title: Teamwork, conflict and negotiation
blurb: Listen to team concerns, stay calm in conflict, confront and de-escalate well, negotiate, advocate and contribute to the team.
question: Two nurses start arguing loudly at the nurses' station about who should take a new admission, in front of patients and visitors. As the nurse in charge, what should you do first?

teach.h: Conflict is normal; how you handle it matters
teach.body: Disagreement in busy teams is normal and can improve care when handled well. Code 8 asks nurses to work cooperatively: respect colleagues' contributions (8.1), communicate effectively (8.2) and work with colleagues to preserve safety (8.5). Code 9.3 says to deal with differences of professional opinion by discussion and informed debate, respecting others' views and behaving professionally. In plain English: argue about the care, not the person, and never in front of patients.

teach.h: Handling a conflict in the team

steps.label: Listen
steps.sub: each person's concern, reflect it back

head: Skill
What it sounds like
rows: 'It sounds as if the late shifts are hard. Tell me more.'
'When handover is late, the day team can't start obs.'
'I can see you're upset. Let's talk somewhere quieter.'
'You need a bed; I need her safe. Could we move Mr B?'
'Mr K has views on this; Mr K, would you explain?'

teach.body: Confronting a colleague is not attacking them. Choose a private place and a calm moment, describe the specific behaviour you saw, say what effect it has on patients or the team, then ask for their view and agree what will change. Keep to facts, not labels ('you're lazy'). If the problem continues or patients are at risk, escalate through the proper route.

Negotiation looks for a solution that meets both sides' real needs: a site manager needs a bed, the nurse needs a vulnerable patient kept safe, so offering an alternative can satisfy both. Advocacy means making sure the person's own voice and wishes are heard, especially when they are vulnerable (Code 3.4 act as an advocate for the vulnerable). Good advocacy invites the person to speak rather than speaking over them.

Proficiency P1.18 asks nurses to contribute effectively and proactively in an interdisciplinary team. Nurses often know most about how a person is at night or day to day, so they must share it: keep colleagues informed (Code 8.3) and share information to identify and reduce risk (8.6). P5.10 adds contributing to supervision and team reflection: regular, facilitated reflection helps teams understand each other and improve practice.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Charge Nurse Kwame at night
teach.body: At 23:00 the site manager asks Kwame to move Mrs Lowry, 88, who has delirium, to another ward to free a bed. Kwame explains calmly that a night move could worsen her confusion and risk a fall, and proposes moving a stable patient awaiting discharge instead. The site manager agrees. Kwame records the discussion. He has negotiated, advocated for a vulnerable patient and kept the relationship professional.

teach.text: De-escalation fails in front of an audience. Move the conversation somewhere quieter, keep a safe distance and an exit, and acknowledge feelings before discussing facts.

items: Code 9.3: resolve differences of professional opinion by discussion and informed debate.
Stay calm, move conflict away from patients, listen and reflect back concerns.
Confront privately and specifically about behaviour and its effect; escalate if unresolved or unsafe.
Negotiate for solutions that meet both sides' needs; advocate so the person's own voice is heard.
Share what you know in the MDT (P1.18) and take part in team reflection (P5.10).

summary: You can now listen actively to colleagues, keep a calm presence, confront and de-escalate conflict appropriately, negotiate and advocate for vulnerable people, and escalate when needed. You can also contribute proactively to interdisciplinary decisions and team reflection.

A.q: According to Code 9.3, how should nurses deal with differences of professional opinion with colleagues?
options: By asking the most senior person to decide
By recording the disagreement in the notes
By following the majority view of the team
By discussion and informed debate
A.why: Code 9.3: deal with differences of professional opinion with colleagues by discussion and informed debate, respecting their views and opinions and behaving in a professional way at all times.

whyNot.0: Seniority alone does not resolve professional disagreement under the Code.
whyNot.1: Disputes between staff are not recorded in the patient's notes as a resolution method.
whyNot.2: A majority view is not the Code's standard; informed debate is.

A.q: A colleague says the new shift pattern is making her childcare impossible. Which response best shows active listening?
options: 'Everyone has to work the same pattern, I'm afraid.'
'The new shifts sound hard. Can you tell me more?'
'Have you thought about changing to part-time hours?'
'You should raise that with the ward manager, really.'
A.why: Active listening gives full attention, reflects the concern back and invites the person to say more before solutions are discussed (AnnexA.4.2.2).

whyNot.0: This closes the conversation without hearing the concern.
whyNot.2: Jumping to a solution skips understanding her concern.
whyNot.3: Redirecting at once does not listen to her concern.

A.q: Two nurses begin arguing loudly at the nurses' station in front of patients. What should the nurse in charge do first?
options: Tell them both off in front of everyone
Leave it until the end of the shift and see
Report both to the ward manager by email later
Calmly ask them to talk it over in the office
A.why: A calm presence and moving the conflict to a private place protects patients' dignity and professionalism and allows the issue to be resolved (AnnexA.4.2.3; Code 20.1).

whyNot.0: Public reprimand escalates the conflict and is unprofessional.
whyNot.1: Leaving it continues the disruption and patients' discomfort.
whyNot.2: An email does not stop the immediate conflict.

B.q: Danny has noticed that a colleague often hands over late, delaying the morning observations. What is the most effective confrontation strategy?
options: Mention it in a group message to the team
Complain about her to other staff at the break
Talk privately about the effect on patients
Hand over late to her in return next time
B.why: Effective confrontation is private, specific and focused on behaviour and its impact on patients, inviting the other person's view and agreeing a solution (AnnexA.4.2.4; Code 8).

whyNot.0: Public group messages embarrass and are less likely to change behaviour.
whyNot.1: Gossip damages relationships and solves nothing.
whyNot.3: Retaliation harms patients and the team.

B.q: At 23:00, the site manager asks to move Mrs Lowry, who has delirium, to another ward. What is the best negotiation?
options: Agree straight away to avoid conflict
Explain the risk; propose moving a stable patient
Refuse and end the conversation there and then
Ask Mrs Lowry's family to refuse the move for her
B.why: Negotiation explores both parties' needs: the manager needs a bed; the nurse needs to protect a vulnerable patient. Offering an alternative meets both (AnnexA.4.2.6.1; Code 3.4).

whyNot.0: Agreeing without raising the risk fails to advocate for the patient.
whyNot.2: Refusing without discussion does not solve the bed problem.
whyNot.3: Using the family to block the move avoids professional negotiation.

B.q: In a ward round, the team discusses Mr Kapoor's operation while he lies listening. He told the nurse earlier he has doubts. What is the best advocacy?
options: Say Mr Kapoor has views and invite him to explain
Tell the team his doubts on his behalf afterwards
Wait until the team leaves, then reassure him
Ask the consultant to decide what is best for him
B.why: Advocacy means making sure the person's own voice is heard in decisions about their care (AnnexA.4.2.6.3; Code 3.4). Inviting him to speak supports his autonomy.

whyNot.1: Speaking for him later is less empowering than enabling him to speak now.
whyNot.2: Reassurance afterwards leaves his doubts out of the decision.
whyNot.3: This removes his voice from a decision about his own care.

C.q: At a discharge planning meeting, the physiotherapist reports Mrs Ansah walks safely. Nurse Femi has seen her become confused and unsteady each night. What should he do?
options: Stay quiet, as the physio has already assessed her mobility
Tell Mrs Ansah's family after the meeting
Share what he saw and ask for the plan to be reviewed
Record it in the notes after the meeting
C.why: Nurses contribute proactively in the interdisciplinary team (P1.18) and share information to identify and reduce risk (Code 8.6). New night-time confusion may indicate delirium and affects safe discharge.

whyNot.0: Staying silent withholds information that affects her safety.
whyNot.1: The family should be informed, but the team making the decision needs the information now.
whyNot.3: Recording it later means the decision is made without it.

C.q: A visitor shouts at a nurse at the nurses' station because his father's meal was late. Other patients are watching. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Tell him to calm down or security will be called
Calmly acknowledge his frustration; offer a quieter place
Explain that the ward is short-staffed and it isn't her fault
Walk away until he has calmed down by himself
C.why: De-escalation uses a calm tone and non-threatening body language, acknowledges the person's feelings and moves the conversation away from an audience, keeping a safe distance and exit route (AnnexA.4.2.5).

whyNot.0: An early threat is likely to escalate the situation.
whyNot.2: A defensive explanation before acknowledging his concern may inflame him.
whyNot.3: Walking away leaves him unheard and may escalate.

C.q: Two healthcare assistants refuse to work together. The nurse in charge has spoken to both, but call bells in their bay are now going unanswered. What should she do?
options: Leave them to sort it out themselves
Swap them to opposite shifts without telling anybody else
Take over all their patients herself for the shift
Ensure patients get care and escalate to the ward manager
C.why: Patients come first: their care must be secured now (Code 1.2; standard 16, act without delay). Where direct discussion has not resolved a conflict that affects care, it should be escalated through appropriate procedures (AnnexA.4.2.6.2).

whyNot.0: Leaving it allows ongoing risk to patients.
whyNot.1: Changing rotas covertly does not address the conflict and bypasses management.
whyNot.2: Taking on all their patients is unsafe and does not resolve the conflict.

reteach.title: Turn down the heat
reteach.question: When a pan boils over, do you turn up the heat or take it off the hob?

blocks.body: In any conflict, your first job is to lower the temperature: steady voice, open posture, a quieter place, and genuine acknowledgement of how the other person feels. Only then can you talk facts, find what each side really needs, and agree a way forward. If it cannot be solved between you, or patients are at risk, escalate.

blocks.text: Advocacy is not speaking instead of the person; it is making sure their own voice is heard.

explain.body: Give full attention, reflect back what you hear and invite the person to say more before offering solutions (AnnexA.4.2.2).

test.q: Which phrase is the best example of reflecting back in active listening?
options: 'So you feel your ideas go unheard?'
'I know exactly how you feel about it.'
'Most nurses feel like that at first.'
'Let's not dwell on it.'
test.why: Reflecting back restates the person's concern to check understanding and show it has been heard (AnnexA.4.2.2).

whyNot.1: Claiming to know how someone feels can dismiss their experience.

explain.body: Calm tone, non-threatening body language, acknowledge feelings, move away from an audience, keep a safe distance and exit (AnnexA.4.2.5).

test.q: Which action is most likely to help de-escalate an angry person?
options: Acknowledging their feelings in a calm voice
Standing close and pointing at the rules poster
Explaining they are upsetting other patients
Telling them to lower their voice immediately
test.why: Acknowledging feelings calmly is central to de-escalation (AnnexA.4.2.5).

whyNot.1: Standing close and pointing feels threatening.
whyNot.3: Commands often escalate rather than calm.

explain.body: Identify each side's underlying needs and look for an option that meets both. Offer alternatives rather than a flat yes or no (AnnexA.4.2.6.1).

test.q: What is the key feature of effective negotiation?
options: Holding firm until the other side finally gives in
Finding an option meeting both sides' needs
Asking a manager to decide straight away
Agreeing quickly to keep the peace
test.why: Effective negotiation explores each side's underlying needs and seeks a solution that meets both (AnnexA.4.2.6.1).

whyNot.0: Win-lose positions damage relationships and miss better solutions.
whyNot.3: Giving in quickly may sacrifice patient safety.

explain.body: Regular, facilitated team reflection lets staff share experiences, understand each other's views and agree improvements (P5.10; AnnexA.4.1.4).

test.q: A team has had tension after a difficult month. Which step best reflects proficiency P5.10?
options: Ask each person to write a statement
Move the most vocal staff to other wards for now
Set up regular, facilitated team reflection
Agree not to discuss the past month again
test.why: P5.10 asks nurses to contribute to supervision and team reflection to improve practice; facilitated reflection supports learning and relationships.

whyNot.0: Written statements suit investigations, not team learning.
whyNot.1: Moving staff does not address the underlying issues.
